title: The Real Reason Chinese AI Is Winning the Global South
gist: Foreign Policy op-ed excerpt (Lizzi C. Lee, Zhuoning Li) arguing Chinese open-weight models, led by Alibaba's Qwen, are winning the global south because their free, locally runnable model beats the API-metered walled gardens of OpenAI and Anthropic; unlike Belt and Road, this influence is pulled by developers rather than pushed by Beijing, making it more organic and harder to dislodge.

insights.claim: Alibaba's Qwen has 151,448 derivative models on Hugging Face, a repository footprint 4.7 times that of Meta's Llama and almost double that of Google's Gemma.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Qwen has become the default base model for open-source developers, an ecosystem moat for Alibaba.
insights.quote: Alibaba’s Qwen, for example, boasts 151,448 derivatives on Hugging Face.

insights.claim: Qwen draws 39.6 million monthly downloads in GGUF, a lightweight format optimized for local hardware, versus 7.5 million for Llama.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Heavy local/edge usage signals demand for on-device inference outside US cloud APIs.
insights.quote: It also draws 39.6 million monthly downloads of GGUF, a lightweight format optimized for local hardware, far ahead of Llama’s 7.5 million.

insights.claim: Top US AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic still largely follow a walled-garden model with access metered through APIs and subscriptions, which is a harder sell in cost-sensitive global south markets.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: US closed-model monetization may cede emerging-market share to free Chinese open weights, capping TAM.
insights.quote: That is a harder sell in cost-sensitive markets across the global south.

insights.claim: Chinese open-weight models offer the global south a feasible alternative and are being viewed, per Stanford HAI analysts, as next-generation digital infrastructure with built-in geopolitical implications.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
entities: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
insights.so_what: AI model choice is becoming infrastructure lock-in with geopolitical consequences.
insights.quote: a next generation of digital infrastructure with geopolitical implications built in

insights.claim: Unlike the Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese AI's spread does not need to be pushed by the central government; Beijing is instead being pulled in by global developers.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Bottom-up adoption is harder for US policy (export controls, sanctions) to reverse than state-led projects.
insights.quote: Chinese AI does not need to be pushed by the central government. If anything, Beijing is being pulled in by developers globally.

insights.claim: Adoption of Chinese open-weight AI began well before Xi Jinping's pitch to global south leaders at the Shanghai World AI Conference in July, indicating the trend is market-led rather than policy-led.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Policy announcements are lagging, not leading, indicators of Chinese AI uptake.
insights.quote: Adoption began well before Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered his now-famous pitch

insights.claim: Because it is organic, China's AI-driven geopolitical influence in the global south may be much harder to dislodge than state-pushed initiatives.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Expect durable Chinese AI ecosystem entrenchment in emerging markets; US competitors face sticky incumbency.
insights.quote: The geopolitical influence may be more organic and therefore much harder to dislodge.
